This is an ambitious aim, and the combination of methods proposed is cutting-edge. The investigator team has considerable expertise in IDRs, especially with respect to biomolecular condensates. The data set is an untapped resource for understanding protein structure/function, so that aspect of the proposal is quite exciting. There are several weaknesses, unfortunately, that drive my major skepticism for the reliability of the insights that would result from the proposed work. Most importantly, the proposal fails to recognize the massively complicating factor that pressure will play in the data set, the scientific questions posed, and the methods they propose to use. They don’t plan to simulate pressure due to the absence of a pressure-validated course-grained model, yet they fail to realize that the algorithms they will use to predict intrinsic disorder in the first place are not parameterized in any way to account for the pressure effects on protein structure. The IDR prediction from genetic data is the first step in the entire project, so even a moderate error in that prediction will likely cascade into a host of spurious outputs. I would feel a little bit better about a protein-based analysis of this data set if the goal were to study well-structured proteins with high homology, as there is at least ample data for comparision of well-folded proteins from extremophiles in the PDB, but the plan to examin IDRs, for which the predictive models should not be trusted for extremophilic proteins, is especially worrisome to me.

review_text: The proposal investigates intrinsically disordered protein regions as environmental sensors by combining metagenomic data with structure prediction and molecular dynamics simulations. The project features a multidisciplinary team executing a logical workflow to produce predictive models and a comprehensive sequence database with justified computational resource requests. The methodology emphasizes generating new simulation data from a narrow selection of genomic resources rather than synthesizing diverse existing datasets and the massive scope presents execution risks.
strengths_text: The research establishes a relevant connection between protein biophysics and environmental adaptation. The multidisciplinary team utilizes a logical progression of tasks to produce broadly applicable predictive models alongside adequately justified resource allocations.
weakness_text: The generation of massive simulation data from two genomic databases conflicts with the program objective of synthesizing heterogeneous existing datasets. The broad scope encompassing database construction alongside deep learning model training and generative design presents significant feasibility risks for the proposed duration.
original_review_text: This proposal aims to systematically characterize intrinsically disordered protein regions (IDRs) as environmental sensors using metagenomic data from Tara Oceans and derivative resources (Ocean Gene Atlas v2.0, OceanDNA), combined with structure prediction (ESMFold/AlphaFold3), IDR-specific tools (Metapredict, CIDER, ALBATROSS), and extensive coarse-grained MD simulations analyzed via deep learning. From the perspective of a reviewer with expertise in crosslinking mass spectrometry, proteomics data standards, and network/pathway integration, the proposal is scientifically interesting and clearly interdisciplinary, but it is largely a computational/biophysical modeling and simulation-heavy project rather than a data synthesis project in the sense emphasized by this RFP. The core scientific engine is molecular dynamics simulation (26 million CPU hours, ~440,000 trajectories) layered onto an existing public sequence database, with relatively modest emphasis on integrating truly distinct heterogeneous datasets (e.g., proteomics, interactomes, structural repositories) that would exemplify cross-dataset synthesis. The reliance on a single primary metagenomic resource (OGA2) plus one genomic annotation resource (OceanDNA) is a narrower data landscape than what is typically expected for 'community-scale synthesis integrating distinct datasets.' There is no proteomics validation data (e.g., mass spectrometry-based protein abundance or interaction data) despite the team purportedly including biophysics expertise; incorporating actual experimental structural or interaction datasets (PDB, crosslinking-MS interaction data, AlphaFold DB, BioGRID/STRING/IntAct) would have strengthened the synthesis dimension considerably. The scope is also very ambitious for 24 months—building a comprehensive IDR catalog, running and analyzing hundreds of thousands of simulations, training multiple deep learning architectures (VAEs, GNNs, GANs), and then designing and validating de novo IDR sequences experimentally is an enormous undertaking that risks overpromising relative to the timeline and requested resources. The requested NCEMS resources (staff scientists, CPU hours, storage) are reasonably justified for the simulation and database components, but the plan for experimental validation of designed IDRs is vague ('collaborations with biophysics experts') and not costed or scheduled. Open science commitments are stated only in generic terms (public release of tools/datasets) without specifics on repositories, standards, or workflow reproducibility—an area where this reviewer's domain (data standards, ProteomeXchange, USI, PEFF) would expect more rigor. Overall, the biological question—how IDRs act as environmental sensors under extreme marine conditions—is compelling and novel, and the team composition spans genuinely complementary disciplines, but the project reads more as a large computational biophysics/ML pipeline built on one database than as a multi-dataset, cross-lab synthesis of existing public data as envisioned by this funding mechanism.

target_authors: Keren Lasker; Jerelle A. Joseph; Alex Holehouse
review_text: The proposal investigates environmental adaptation mechanisms by analyzing marine metagenomic datasets to characterize intrinsically disordered protein regions. The conceptual framework leverages large public resources to construct an integrative analytical pipeline exploring molecular emergence. The execution plan relies heavily on generating large amounts of new simulation data rather than synthesizing existing information while presenting an unrealistic timeline and unvalidated model extrapolations.
strengths_text: The project evaluates intrinsically disordered protein regions acting as environmental sensors by analyzing established marine metagenomic databases. The analytical approach combines sequence evaluation, structural modeling and dynamic simulations to produce predictive tools and a sequence database.
weakness_text: The focus on producing substantial new molecular dynamics simulation data misaligns with the primary objective of data synthesis. The 24 month schedule accommodates an excessively broad scope of machine learning development and generative design while the analytical models exclude environmental pressure variables and extrapolation validation.
original_review_text: This proposal aims to leverage large-scale marine metagenomic datasets (Tara Oceans via OGA2, OceanDNA) to characterize intrinsically disordered protein regions (IDRs) as environmental sensors, combining bioinformatic annotation, coarse-grained MD simulation, and deep learning to map sequence-to-function relationships across environmental gradients. The core scientific question—how IDRs mediate environmental adaptation—is compelling and underexplored at this scale, and the use of existing, richly annotated metagenomic resources is appropriate and well-matched to the RFP's synthesis mandate. However, from a data-reuse and computational biology perspective, several concerns arise. First, the project is heavily weighted toward de novo generation of new computational data (~440,000 MD trajectories, 26M CPU hours) rather than synthesis of existing datasets; while MD simulation is not 'experimental' data generation in the traditional sense, this activity dominates the proposed budget and timeline and shifts the project's center of gravity away from data synthesis and toward large-scale simulation production, which may not align cleanly with the call's emphasis on integrating existing data. Second, the 24-month timeline for building a comprehensive IDR catalog across ~55 million sequences, running hundreds of thousands of simulations, developing multiple deep learning models (VAEs, GNNs, GANs), and then designing/validating de novo IDR sequences is extremely ambitious and likely unrealistic without significant unstated preliminary infrastructure. Third, the description of team composition, institutional diversity, and career-stage representation is vague—there is no explicit list of team members, their specific roles, or how trainees will be incorporated into research activities beyond generic mentions. Fourth, open science commitments (data/workflow deposition standards, community accessibility of the resulting IDR database) are asserted but not operationalized with specific repositories, licensing, or interoperability standards (e.g., FAIR principles, existing IDR/protein community standards). The reliance on many disparate tools (ESMFold, AlphaFold3, Chainsaw, Metapredict, ALBATROSS, CIDER, Mpipi-Recharge) is reasonable but the pipeline's end-to-end validation—particularly extrapolating ALBATROSS-derived physiological state predictions to extreme pressure/salinity/temperature conditions with only partial simulation coverage (no pressure modeling)—raises rigor concerns. Overall, this is an interesting synthesis-adjacent idea with genuine potential for novel insight into an underexplored aspect of environmental molecular biology, but its scope, timeline feasibility, and the balance between data synthesis versus new computational data generation need substantial reconsideration.
rephrased_review: The proposal investigates environmental adaptation mechanisms by analyzing marine metagenomic datasets to characterize intrinsically disordered protein regions. original_review_text: This proposal seeks to characterize intrinsically disordered proteins (IDRs) as environmental sensors using Tara Oceans metagenomic data, combining bioinformatics annotation, coarse-grained simulation, and machine learning to map sequence-structure-environment relationships. The topic is timely and fits well within the biophysics-meets-data-synthesis space that this working group model favors. From a protein biophysics/allostery perspective, the conceptual framing of IDRs as conformational sensors that respond to physicochemical gradients is scientifically sound and resonates with established principles of disorder-based regulation, though the emergent phenomena angle here is more implicit (ensemble-level conformational plasticity as an adaptive trait) rather than an explicit order-parameter or emergent-property framework. The three-activity structure (catalog, simulate, mechanistically map) is logical, but the scope is extremely ambitious: annotating tens of millions of sequences, running ~440,000 coarse-grained MD trajectories, and then building generative models for design within 24 months. This is a very large computational undertaking, and while the resource request is scaled accordingly, the plan does not sufficiently address failure modes—e.g., what happens if temperature/salinity coarse-grained models do not generalize, or if the environmental metadata linked to protein abundance is too coarse to produce statistically robust correlations given confounds like phylogeny and taxonomic composition. The use of ALBATROSS outside its training regime (extreme conditions) is acknowledged as a limitation but the proposed correction (custom in-house temperature model) is not detailed with validation benchmarks. The heavy reliance on unpublished/proprietary in-house coarse-grained models for temperature effects also raises questions about reproducibility and rigor, since these are not established, peer-validated tools like Mpipi-Recharge. The synthesis component (leveraging OGA2, OceanDNA, existing structure predictors) is strong and clearly appropriate for a working-group scale, exceeding what a single lab could realistically process. Team composition (metagenomics, biophysics, cell biology, deep learning) is well-matched to the goals. Open science commitments are stated at a high level (public release of datasets/tools) but lack detail on specific repositories, licensing, or workflow standards. Overall this is an interesting, large-scale synthesis proposal with a coherent narrative, though the ambition-to-timeline ratio and insufficient methodological validation details around novel coarse-grained models are concerning.

original_review_text: This proposal seeks to systematically catalog and characterize intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) in marine proteins using Tara Oceans metagenomic data, combining bioinformatic annotation, coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations, and deep learning to link IDR biophysical properties to environmental adaptation. As a reviewer with a background in computational protein biophysics, molecular topology, and simulation-based structural characterization, I find the conceptual premise compelling: IDRs as environmentally responsive sensors is an underexplored area, and the availability of large, geographically and environmentally annotated metagenomic datasets (OGA2, OceanDNA) is a genuine opportunity for synthesis-style research that individual lab-scale studies could not undertake. The project correctly identifies that no single lab possesses the combined expertise in metagenomics curation, coarse-grained biophysical simulation, and machine learning needed to execute this work, and the team composition (bioinformatics, biophysics, ML) is appropriate to that end. However, several methodological concerns temper my enthusiasm. The use of ALBATROSS and Mpipi-family coarse-grained models to infer IDR ensemble properties under extreme, non-physiological conditions (deep-sea pressure, temperature, salinity) is scientifically risky since these tools and force fields were parameterized on data collected under near-ambient conditions; the proposal acknowledges this limitation but the described mitigation (an in-house temperature model, omission of pressure entirely) is thin on validation strategy. Given my group's experience with coarse-grained polymer models for biomolecules, I would want to see explicit benchmarking against any experimental or all-atom reference data before drawing conclusions about environmental conformational adaptation. The scale of computation proposed (~440,000 trajectories, 26M CPU-hours) within a 24-month window, alongside database construction, feature extraction, and downstream generative design work, appears highly ambitious and likely underestimates the time needed for quality control, especially for a team assembled around this specific proposal without extensive prior collaborative history. The synthesis and data-identification aspects are strong: the datasets are clearly named, sized, and publicly available, and the working group directly requires NCEMS-scale computational and staff support that would be unattainable for any individual lab. Open science commitments are stated but underspecified regarding workflow reproducibility, versioning, and community standards. Overall, this is an interesting, well-motivated synthesis proposal with real scientific merit, but it would benefit from a more conservative scope, stronger validation planning for extreme-condition simulations, and a clearer data/workflow release plan.

original_review_text: This proposal seeks to characterize intrinsically disordered protein regions (IDRs) as environmental sensors using Tara Oceans metagenomic data, combining bioinformatic annotation, coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations, and deep learning-based representation learning. The scientific premise is compelling: IDRs are indeed strong candidates for encoding environmentally responsive conformational behavior, and the deep sea provides a natural gradient of physicochemical stressors ideal for such analysis. The team composition (metagenomics, biophysics/simulation, deep learning) is well matched to the multi-stage pipeline described. From a computational systems perspective, the scale of the proposed simulation campaign (~440,000 trajectories, 26M CPU hours) is substantial and plausibly requires the kind of infrastructure and staff support NCEMS could provide, which strengthens the case for centralized resource allocation rather than single-lab execution. The reliance on public datasets (OGA2, OceanDNA) and established prediction tools (ESMFold, AlphaFold3, Metapredict, ALBATROSS, Mpipi-Recharge, Chainsaw) reflects a reasonable synthesis-oriented strategy, repurposing existing sequence/structure resources rather than generating new experimental data. That said, several aspects raise concern from a computational and data-engineering standpoint. The claim that ALBATROSS predictions will be supplemented with a 'custom in-house model' for temperature effects is not well substantiated; validation of this novel model, and how its outputs will be reconciled quantitatively with ALBATROSS-derived salt gradient predictions, is not addressed. The workflow chains together many predictive models (structure prediction, domain detection, IDR prediction, biophysical property prediction) each with its own error profile, and no discussion is provided on how uncertainty propagates through this pipeline, which is a significant risk to the validity of downstream 'universal adaptation rules.' The computational budget for ~440,000 simulation trajectories within a 24-month timeline, alongside development of GNN/VAE/GAN-based analysis pipelines and a generative design framework, seems highly ambitious; per-trajectory simulation, storage, and analysis throughput estimates are not detailed enough to assess feasibility. Additionally, the proposal states experimental validation of designed IDR sequences will occur 'through collaborations with biophysics experts,' but no such experimental partner or capability is described in the team, undermining confidence in that final validation step. Overall, the proposal is intellectually interesting and technically ambitious, aligning reasonably well with the synthesis-based, cross-disciplinary mandate of the call, but the technical execution plan needs tighter specification, particularly around computational scaling, model validation, and uncertainty quantification across the multi-tool pipeline.

original_review_text:
This proposal addresses an interesting and potentially important question: whether intrinsically disordered regions in marine proteins encode adaptive biophysical features across environmental gradients such as temperature, salinity, and depth. The central idea is well aligned with synthesis science in that it seeks to integrate large public metagenomic resources with protein biophysics, environmental metadata, simulations, and machine learning. The use of Tara Oceans-derived Ocean Gene Atlas and OceanDNA resources is appropriate, and the proposed catalog of marine IDRs linked to environmental variables could become a valuable community resource if implemented with strong provenance, standardized identifiers, and reproducible workflows.

The proposal is strongest in its conceptual framing and multidisciplinary ambition. IDRs are plausible mediators of physicochemical sensing, and marine metagenomic datasets provide a compelling natural experiment for discovering sequence-level adaptation. The proposed combination of disorder prediction, protein annotation, environmental metadata integration, coarse-grained simulations, and representation learning could reveal patterns that are not accessible from single-protein studies. The project also clearly requires expertise beyond a single laboratory, especially at the interface of metagenomics, IDR biophysics, and large-scale computation.

However, the approach is substantially over-scoped and under-specified in several critical areas. The plan to predict structures for tens of millions of proteins using ESMFold and AlphaFold3, annotate domains, identify IDRs, link proteins to environmental and genomic contexts, simulate representative IDRs at very large scale, and then build generative design models within 24 months is not convincingly feasible. The requested 440,000 molecular dynamics trajectories and 26 million CPU hours may be technically possible, but the proposal does not provide enough detail on prioritization, benchmarking, quality control, uncertainty propagation, or criteria for success. There is also a risk that the analysis will be dominated by artifacts from metagenomic assembly, gene prediction, taxonomic composition, protein abundance estimation, and environmental covariation rather than true IDR adaptation. The proposal would benefit from a clearer statistical design that distinguishes adaptation from phylogenetic relatedness, ecological stratification, gene family composition, and sampling bias.

A major rigor concern is that the proposal relies heavily on computational predictors and simulations whose validity for highly divergent marine sequences and extreme environmental conditions is uncertain. The applicants acknowledge limitations of ALBATROSS and pressure modeling, but they do not provide a sufficiently detailed validation strategy. Pressure is central to the deep-sea motivation but is explicitly not simulated, weakening the connection between the proposed biophysical modeling and the stated environmental niche. Similarly, the plan to use AlphaFold3 broadly is not well justified for IDRs, and ordered-domain structure prediction at this scale may consume substantial effort without directly answering the IDR adaptation question. The machine learning component is also described in broad terms, listing variational autoencoders, graph neural networks, and generative adversarial networks without a clear model-selection rationale, training labels, negative controls, validation metrics, or interpretability plan.

The proposal is appropriate for a synthesis call in that it is primarily based on public data, but it includes a statement that designed sequences will be tested computationally and experimentally through collaborations. New experimental testing would fall outside the intended scope of this mechanism unless clearly excluded from NCEMS-supported work. The open science commitment is also not sufficiently developed. The proposal promises public release of databases, tools, and datasets, but it does not specify repositories, metadata standards, versioning, persistent identifiers, workflow systems, licensing, or policies for community reuse. Given the scale of the proposed derived resources, attention to provenance and interoperability is essential.

Overall, this is a creative and potentially high-impact synthesis concept, but the current plan is too ambitious and lacks sufficient methodological specificity for confident execution. A more compelling version would focus on a tractable subset of protein families or environmental gradients, define rigorous controls for phylogeny and sampling bias, establish validation benchmarks using experimentally characterized IDRs and known extremophile proteins, and provide a concrete open-science and data-standardization plan.

original_review_text:
This proposal addresses an interesting and potentially important question: whether intrinsically disordered regions in marine proteins exhibit systematic sequence and biophysical adaptations across environmental gradients such as temperature and salinity. The concept is well aligned with synthesis science in that it aims to integrate public metagenomic resources, environmental metadata, protein disorder prediction, simulation-derived biophysical annotations, and machine learning. The topic is significant, and the proposed team expertise in metagenomics, protein biophysics, and machine learning is appropriate for a working group mechanism.

However, the proposal is substantially weakened by overreach and insufficient methodological specificity. The plan appears to scale from tens of millions of metagenomic protein sequences to structure prediction, disorder annotation, homolog grouping, hundreds of thousands of molecular dynamics trajectories, latent-space modeling, evolutionary trajectory inference, and de novo design within 24 months. Several components are not realistically scoped. Predicting structures for approximately 55 million proteins using ESMFold and AlphaFold3 is not clearly feasible, nor is it clear that AlphaFold3 can be used at this scale under current access and licensing constraints. The proposed 440,000 molecular dynamics trajectories and 26 million CPU hours are ambitious, but the proposal does not provide enough detail on trajectory length, convergence criteria, sampling strategy, sequence selection, reproducibility, or how simulation outputs will be validated. The deep sea is framed as a central motivation, yet pressure, one of the defining deep-sea variables, is explicitly not simulated, and the depth ranges described are inconsistent across the proposal.

The biological inference is also underdeveloped. Linking IDR features to environmental adaptation from metagenomic occurrence and abundance data is challenging because of strong confounding by taxonomy, phylogeny, gene function, genome composition, assembly quality, ORF prediction, and sampling depth. The proposal mentions orthologs but does not provide a rigorous comparative phylogenetic framework to distinguish adaptation from shared ancestry or community composition effects. Functional assignments for IDRs in fragmented metagenomic proteins are likely to be noisy, and the proposal does not adequately describe quality control, redundancy reduction, domain boundary uncertainty, disorder predictor calibration for metagenomic proteins, or benchmarking against known extremophile proteins. The machine learning sections rely heavily on broad lists of model classes rather than well-defined tasks, labels, baselines, evaluation metrics, and controls. This creates a risk that the work will produce correlations and embeddings without interpretable or biologically robust conclusions.

There is also a compliance concern with the call. The proposal mostly uses public data, but Activity 3 states that designed IDRs will be tested computationally and experimentally through collaborations. New experimental testing would not fit the stated requirement that the project does not generate new experimental data. If experimental validation is external and not supported by this project, that boundary should be clearly stated; otherwise this is a material mismatch. The open science commitment is positive in spirit but lacks concrete details about repositories, workflow systems, metadata standards, licensing, versioning, and long-term maintenance of the proposed database and tools.

Overall, the proposal is creative and relevant, but it needs substantial tightening. A stronger version would narrow the scale, define a robust comparative framework controlling for taxonomy and protein family, focus on a tractable subset of well-annotated homologous protein families or environmental gradients, clarify which public data products and metadata will be used, remove or clearly separate experimental work, and provide concrete open-science and reproducibility plans.

original_review_text:
This proposal addresses an interesting and timely question: whether intrinsically disordered regions in marine proteins encode generalizable molecular adaptations to temperature, salinity, depth, and other environmental gradients. The idea of synthesizing Tara Oceans/Ocean Gene Atlas protein sequences with environmental metadata, IDR predictors, coarse-grained simulations, and machine learning is well aligned with the spirit of community-scale synthesis and could produce a useful public resource for the disorder and marine biology communities. The proposal is strongest in its conceptual framing and in recognizing that IDRs may act as emergent molecular sensors whose ensemble properties depend on sequence composition and environment. It also identifies major public datasets and proposes integrative analyses that would be difficult for a single laboratory to execute.

However, the work plan is substantially overextended and contains several methodological and programmatic weaknesses. The proposal moves from cataloging tens of millions of proteins, to structure prediction, to 440,000 molecular dynamics trajectories, to deep generative modeling, to de novo IDR design, and even experimental testing within 24 months. This is not sufficiently prioritized. Several steps are underspecified, including how homologous IDRs will be identified robustly in fragmented metagenomic assemblies, how taxonomic and phylogenetic confounding will be separated from environmental adaptation, how protein abundance and environmental metadata will be normalized, and how false discovery will be controlled when testing many sequence-environment associations. The plan to apply AlphaFold3/ESMFold broadly to tens of millions of proteins is not realistic or clearly necessary for IDR-focused questions. The simulation component is also not fully convincing: pressure, one of the central deep-sea variables motivating the project, is explicitly not simulated; salinity variation in the selected data is relatively modest; and the coarse-grained models may not be validated outside near-physiological conditions. The machine learning sections list many advanced architectures but do not define concrete prediction tasks, training/validation splits, baselines, uncertainty estimates, or criteria for mechanistic interpretation.

The proposal is responsive to the call in its use of public metagenomic data and in its need for cross-disciplinary expertise, but its fit is weakened by the inclusion of experimental testing of designed IDRs and by the large-scale generation of new simulation datasets that may dominate the effort rather than synthesis of existing data. Computationally derived data can be appropriate for this program, but the proposal should more clearly distinguish synthesis, reanalysis, and model-derived predictions from new data generation. The open science intent is positive, including public release of tools and databases, but policies for reproducibility, workflow sharing, licensing, metadata standards, and trainee participation are not developed in sufficient detail. Overall, this is a compelling idea with potentially high impact, but the current proposal needs sharper hypotheses, a more feasible and staged analysis plan, clearer validation strategy, and stronger alignment with the synthesis-only constraints of the call.

original_review_text:
This proposal addresses an interesting and potentially important question: whether intrinsically disordered regions in marine proteins show systematic sequence and biophysical adaptations across environmental gradients, and whether these adaptations can reveal general principles of molecular environmental sensing. The use of Tara Oceans/Ocean Gene Atlas and associated environmental metadata is well aligned with a synthesis-oriented call, and the conceptual connection between sequence composition, conformational ensembles, and environmental variables is compelling. The proposal is strongest in its ambition to integrate metagenomics, IDR biophysics, coarse-grained modeling, and machine learning at a scale not feasible for a single laboratory.

However, the approach is currently overextended and insufficiently constrained. The plan to annotate tens of millions of proteins, predict structures using ESMFold/AlphaFold3, identify domains and IDRs, simulate representative IDRs across environmental conditions, and then infer evolutionary trajectories and design new IDRs within 24 months is not well justified. Several technical assumptions need much more careful treatment. Metagenomic protein sequences are often fragmented, unevenly sampled, taxonomically confounded, and linked to environmental parameters through community abundance rather than organism-specific physiology. The proposal does not adequately explain how it will distinguish IDR adaptation from phylogenetic signal, gene family composition, expression/abundance bias, or assembly/annotation artifacts. The reliance on predictors trained largely on model-organism or physiological-condition data may be problematic for marine metagenomic proteins and extreme environments. The simulation plan is also only partially matched to the motivating environmental gradients: pressure is central to the deep-sea rationale but explicitly excluded, and the temperature and salt models require clearer validation against experimental or high-resolution simulation benchmarks.

A further concern is fit to the call. The core data sources are public and appropriate, but the proposal includes very large-scale new simulations, de novo design, and possible experimental testing. Computational data generation can be appropriate if it supports synthesis, but here the simulation and design components risk becoming the dominant activity rather than a synthesis of existing data. The proposal would be stronger if it more clearly defined a tractable biological question, a limited set of protein families or ecological contrasts, statistical controls for phylogeny and environment, and concrete validation benchmarks. The open science and training plans are also underdeveloped relative to the expectations of the call.

Overall, this is a creative, multidisciplinary proposal with a strong public-data foundation and a potentially high payoff, but it needs sharper hypotheses, stronger statistical and biophysical validation, better attention to metagenomic confounders, and a more realistic scope.

original_review_text:
This proposal addresses an interesting and potentially important question: whether intrinsically disordered protein regions exhibit systematic sequence and biophysical adaptations across marine environmental gradients. The focus on IDRs as molecular sensors is well aligned with emergence in molecular and cellular biosciences, since the relevant properties arise from ensembles, sequence composition, environmental context, and evolutionary selection rather than from single static structures. The proposal also makes appropriate use of large public resources, particularly Tara Oceans-derived datasets through Ocean Gene Atlas v2.0 and OceanDNA, and it clearly requires expertise spanning metagenomics, protein biophysics, molecular simulation, and machine learning.

The strongest aspect is the conceptual integration of environmental metagenomics with IDR biophysics. If successful, a curated catalog linking IDR sequence features, environmental metadata, predicted ensemble properties, and simulation-derived annotations would be a valuable community resource. The proposal also identifies plausible public datasets and describes a working-group structure that is genuinely multidisciplinary. The project has the potential to reveal general principles of protein disorder in environmental adaptation and to produce reusable computational workflows.

However, the approach is substantially overambitious and under-specified in several critical places. The scale of the proposed analysis is enormous: tens of millions of protein sequences, structure prediction using ESMFold and AlphaFold3, IDR prediction, environmental mapping, orthology inference, and approximately 440,000 molecular dynamics trajectories within 24 months. The proposal does not sufficiently justify the feasibility of this scale, nor does it provide a clear prioritization strategy if compute, storage, or annotation quality become limiting. The plan to predict structures for all marine proteins is particularly questionable given the number of sequences, the limited relevance of structure prediction for disordered regions, and the computational costs.

There are also scientific gaps. The proposal emphasizes the deep sea but explicitly does not simulate pressure effects, which is one of the defining environmental variables of the deep sea. Depth is included as a metadata variable, but without pressure modeling the connection between deep-sea adaptation and IDR conformational response is incomplete. Temperature and salinity are better handled, but the proposed statistical framework for separating environmental effects from phylogeny, taxonomy, genome composition, protein abundance, and sampling biases is not well developed. Metagenomic proteins are often fragmented or annotation-poor, and the proposal does not explain how fragment length, assembly quality, contamination, orthology uncertainty, or variable detection thresholds will affect IDR calling and environmental association.

The machine learning component is promising but somewhat generic. Variational autoencoders, graph neural networks, and generative adversarial networks are listed, but the proposal does not specify model inputs, labels, baselines, validation metrics, uncertainty quantification, or how models will avoid learning confounded taxonomic or compositional signals rather than adaptive biophysical principles. The proposed design of novel IDRs is exciting but appears to extend beyond the synthesis mission, especially because the proposal mentions experimental testing through collaborations. The funding call explicitly emphasizes use of existing publicly available data and no new experimental data generation, so this element should either be removed or reframed as computational benchmarking against existing experimental datasets.

Overall, this is a creative and relevant synthesis proposal with strong potential impact, but it would benefit from a narrower, more rigorous, and more explicitly statistical design. A more convincing version would focus on a tractable subset of protein families or environmental gradients, incorporate phylogenetically aware comparative methods, define clear validation datasets, and provide a staged computational plan with decision points. The proposal is responsive to the call in its use of public data and collaborative synthesis, but the feasibility and rigor concerns lower enthusiasm.

original_review_text:
The proposal 'Oceans of Disorder' presents a highly ambitious and conceptually innovative plan to synthesize marine metagenomic data from the Tara Oceans expedition with biophysical simulations and machine learning. The goal is to elucidate how Intrinsically Disordered Proteins (IDRs) adapt to environmental gradients (temperature, salinity, depth) and function as molecular sensors. By integrating massive publicly available datasets (Ocean Gene Atlas v2.0, OceanDNA) with structure prediction (ESMFold, AlphaFold3) and deep learning-based biophysical labeling (ALBATROSS, CIDER), the team aims to map sequence-level IDR adaptations and engineer environmentally resilient proteins. 

From a multi-omics integration and biophysics perspective, this is a fascinating approach. Connecting macroscopic environmental metadata to the microscopic conformational ensembles of IDRs represents a compelling study of emergent phenomena. The combination of coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) and latent space mapping via Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) is methodologically sound and represents state-of-the-art computational biophysics.

However, there are a few areas of concern. First, the proposal relies heavily on OGA2 for 'protein abundance data', which is predominantly inferred from metagenomic or metatranscriptomic data. The incorporation of actual marine metaproteomics datasets (which are increasingly available in public repositories like PRIDE/ProteomeXchange) would provide a critical layer of biological validation to ensure these IDRs are functionally expressed in the claimed environments. Second, the scale of the proposed MD simulations (440,000 trajectories) is colossal. Even with coarse-grained models, managing the I/O, curation, and standardization of these datasets will be a massive informatics challenge. Finally, the proposal briefly mentions that engineered IDR sequences will be 'tested computationally and experimentally through collaborations.' The funding call explicitly states that projects must not generate new experimental data; if these experiments are part of the funded activities, it violates the RFP guidelines. Furthermore, while the applicants commit to open science, the proposal would be strengthened by explicitly adopting community data standards (e.g., standard metadata vocabularies, established database formats) for the resulting IDR catalog.

The integration of public genomic datasets with advanced deep learning and computational biophysics models presents a robust approach to predicting protein structures and engineering resilient sequences. The inclusion of prohibited experimental testing conflicts with funding guidelines while the massive simulation scale and the reliance on transcriptomic proxies over direct proteomics present biological validation and data management risks.
rephrased_strengths: The analytical pipeline effectively combines large public metagenomic datasets with deep learning structure prediction and generative modeling. This methodology establishes a direct connection between macroscopic marine conditions and molecular biophysics to support synthetic biology applications.
rephrased_weakness: The planned experimental testing violates the funding parameters prohibiting new data generation. The reliance on genomic proxies instead of mass spectrometry data restricts biological validation while the immense simulation scale and the required implementation of interoperable database formats present significant data management risks.

original_review_text:
The proposal 'Oceans of Disorder' presents a highly innovative and computationally ambitious plan to synthesize publicly available marine metagenomic data with biophysical simulations to understand the environmental adaptation of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDRs). The integration of large-scale genomic datasets (Tara Oceans) with advanced machine learning (VAEs, GNNs) and molecular dynamics to uncover emergent biophysical properties is scientifically compelling and aligns beautifully with the synthesis mandate of this RFP. The use of latent space representations to model evolutionary trajectories and design novel IDRs is particularly forward-thinking.

However, there are several areas requiring refinement. First, from an evolutionary genomics perspective, the proposal plans to predict 'evolutionary trajectories' of IDRs across environmental gradients but does not explicitly describe how it will account for phylogenetic relationships or ancestry among the microbes. Treating orthologs across environments as independent data points without controlling for phylogeny can lead to spurious correlations. Second, the computational scope is staggering. Generating and analyzing 440,000 coarse-grained MD trajectories in 12 months is an enormous undertaking, even with the requested 26 million CPU hours. The data management and analytical pipeline will need highly standardized, robust workflow managers (e.g., Snakemake, Nextflow), which are not detailed here. Third, the proposal completely omits a plan for training the next generation of data-savvy scientists (graduate students or postdocs), a key requirement of the RFP. The budget only requests Staff Scientists. Finally, while public release of data is mentioned, adherence to specific open science standards, reusable software ecosystems, and FAIR data principles should be elaborated.

The analytical approach links biological sequences to functional traits using latent space representations to support synthetic biology applications. The execution plan introduces schedule risks related to the massive simulation volume and necessitates adjustments to incorporate phylogenetic relationships and robust computational workflows.

rephrased_weakness: The evolutionary modeling risks producing spurious correlations by evaluating orthologs independent of shared ancestry parameters while the budget restricts workforce development strictly to staff scientists. original_review_text:
The proposal 'Oceans of Disorder: Elucidating the Role of Disordered Proteins in Cellular Adaptation' outlines a highly innovative, multidisciplinary approach to understanding how intrinsically disordered proteins (IDRs) adapt to extreme marine environments. By synthesizing publicly available metagenomic data from the Tara Oceans expedition with advanced coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and deep learning, the team aims to map IDR adaptations and define universal principles of protein plasticity. 

From the perspective of computational biophysics and structural modeling, the integration of data-driven modeling and polymer physics to explore conformational ensembles is deeply compelling. The use of chemically specific, one-bead-per-residue coarse-grained models (like the Mpipi-Recharge model) is highly appropriate for sampling the extended timescales required for IDR ensembles, reminiscent of successful approaches in modeling chromosomal structures and complex protein topologies. Furthermore, leveraging AI and deep learning (e.g., GNNs, VAEs, and ESMFold/AlphaFold3) to distill high-dimensional trajectory data into functional biophysical labels is a sophisticated analytical strategy that directly addresses the funding call's objectives.

However, there are a few methodological and logistical areas that warrant scrutiny. First, while the exclusion of pressure from the MD simulations is justified by the lack of a validated coarse-grained model, it inherently limits the comprehensive study of deep-sea adaptations, as hydrostatic pressure is a defining thermodynamic variable of these environments. Second, the computational scale is immense. Running, curating, and analyzing 440,000 MD trajectories within a roughly 12-month window is a monumental task, even with the requested 26 million CPU hours and NCEMS staff support. Finally, the proposal mentions testing designed sequences 'experimentally through collaborations' in Year 2, but since this grant restricts the generation of new experimental data and the timeline is already highly congested, the feasibility and funding mechanisms for this validation phase are vague.
rephrased_review: The proposal outlines a computational approach combining public metagenomic data with molecular dynamics simulations and machine learning to map the adaptation of intrinsically disordered proteins to marine environments. The integration of polymer physics and artificial intelligence to analyze molecular ensembles strongly aligns with the objectives of the funding program. Significant risks involve the immense computational scale planned for a single year along with modeling standard pressure instead of deep ocean conditions and potential grant compliance issues regarding experimental validation.
rephrased_strengths: The project presents a robust analytical pipeline merging molecular dynamics simulations with machine learning to process massive public datasets. This methodology effectively addresses structural emergence by linking macroscopic environmental parameters to protein conformation probabilities.
rephrased_weakness: Executing the proposed simulation volume within a single year presents severe logistical risks. Evaluating deep ocean environments at standard pressure restricts physical accuracy while the planned experimental phase conflicts with program rules regarding new empirical data.

original_review_text: The proposal 'Oceans of Disorder: Elucidating the Role of Disordered Proteins in Cellular Adaptation' outlines a highly innovative community-scale synthesis project to decipher the emergent structural properties of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDRs) across diverse marine environments. By leveraging the Tara Oceans metagenomics datasets alongside advanced deep learning (GNNs, VAEs) and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations, the team aims to establish fundamental principles of environmental sensing in biological systems. As an expert in computational biology, GPU-accelerated algorithms, and mathematical modeling of physiological adaptations, I find the conceptual framework exceptional. The investigators propose a rigorous synthesis of structural biology, bioinformatics, and environmental data that perfectly aligns with the call. The mathematical and generative modeling of evolutionary trajectories is a strong point. However, from a computational efficiency standpoint, the request for 26 million CPU hours for LAMMPS simulations is concerning. Molecular dynamics and deep learning models (GNNs, VAEs) are prime candidates for multi-GPU acceleration, which can yield orders-of-magnitude speedups. The proposal entirely overlooks a GPU-based parallelization strategy, which could significantly mitigate the bottleneck of simulating 440,000 trajectories. Furthermore, while the computational scope is well-detailed, the passing mention of experimental validation in Activity 3 strays slightly from the synthesis-only mandate and lacks methodological detail.

justification_novelty_and_significance: The proposal addresses an important question of comparing DNA, RNA, and protein levels within the same cell. Multimodal data analysis has significant potential to advance knowledge of how DNA, RNA, and protein levels vary across independent cells.. One limitation is that some of the datasets from Dr. Brunk's lab are unpublished. A key feature of the proposal is analyzing multimodal data that simultaneously assess two of three modalities (DNA, RNA, protein) in 7 model cell lines and integrating these datasets with numerous other datasets in these cell lines such as bulk sequencing and proteomics and PERTURB-seq. However approaches to measure RNA and protein such as ECCITE-seq only can measure a limited number of proteins. The cited ECCITE-seq dataset looks to have analyzed RNA content associated with ~50 cell surface proteins. The limitations on the matching of the protein level to DNA or RNA was not sufficiently addressed. The PI mentions FACS+FISH+4i datasets to monitor DNA and  protein levels but there are no references or description for this technique
justification_scope_and_timeline: Goals and timeline are reasonable
justification_data_identification: Data sources are appropriately listed. The proposal clearly demonstrates a synthesis project. One weakness is that five key matched datasets generated by Dr. Brunk are listed listed as being in manuscripts in preparation or under review and were not available.
justification_open_science_commitment: There clearly is a commitment to team science. The nature of the proposal focuses on reproducible science by focusing on 7 cell lines. There is mention of making tools, findings, and pipelines broadly available, but how this will be achieved was not explicitly explained. Judging the commitment to making the data open is difficult to assess as several key datasets are listed as being in manuscripts in preparation or under review. Preprints describing these datasets would have gone a long ways to alleviating this critique.

The rationale of exploiting homogeneous, well-studied model systems to reduce donor/cell-type confounders is sound and pragmatic, and the resulting benchmarking resource could be broadly useful to the community for studying regulatory mechanisms and cellular resource allocation. However, the proposal is fairly generic in its description of computational pipelines and does not specify concrete algorithmic innovations, evaluation metrics, or how single-cell modalities lacking natural pairing (e.g., separate scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, and imaging datasets from different studies) will be computationally aligned at single-cell resolution without ground truth. The data integration challenge (aligning bulk, single-cell, and imaging modalities without shared cell identity) is real and requires cross-lab, cross-domain expertise (computational biology, genomics, imaging, ML), fitting the collaborative and community-scale synthesis mandate. original_review_text: This proposal aims to build multimodal frameworks integrating bulk and single-cell DNA, RNA, protein, and chromatin accessibility data across seven well-characterized cancer cell lines drawn from resources such as DepMap and CCLE. As a structural/molecular topology specialist, I evaluate this primarily on its merits as a synthesis project rather than through the specific lens of protein folding or knotted topology, since the two areas do not directly overlap. The core idea—anchoring multi-omic integration to a small number of extensively profiled, genetically stable cell lines rather than heterogeneous patient cohorts—is a reasonable strategy to reduce donor/cell-type confounds and enable tighter mechanistic inference. The use of exclusively public data (DepMap, CCLE, Perturb-seq, imaging datasets) is appropriate for the synthesis mandate of this call, and the team appears to have the computational/genomics expertise to execute the integration. However, the proposal is thin on methodological specifics: it is unclear what novel algorithmic or statistical strategies will be used to align modalities that are inherently asynchronous (RNA/protein turnover, chromatin state variability at different biological scales), and how 'emergence' as a phenomenon is conceptually framed beyond general statements about regulatory mechanisms and resource allocation. The scope (7 cell lines, multiple omics layers, perturbation screens) is ambitious and could exceed a working-group timeline without more concrete milestones. The connection to emergent phenomena in molecular/cellular biosciences is present but implicit—emergent properties of gene regulatory networks or cellular states are gestured at but not explicitly interrogated as an emergence question per se. Overall this is a solid, data-rich synthesis proposal with clear community utility as a benchmarking resource, though it would benefit from sharper articulation of the specific emergent biological question being addressed and a more detailed integration methodology.

The approach minimizes confounders by utilizing homogeneous model systems and leverages an appropriate mix of machine learning and genomics expertise. The work centers on infrastructure development rather than emergent biological principles and presents an ambitious scope regarding the integration of disparate data modalities across seven cell lines.
strengths_text: The project targets data fragmentation by integrating accessible public resources like DepMap and CCLE. The focus on homogeneous model systems reduces confounding variables related to donor origin and cell type.
weakness_text: The research functions as an infrastructure resource rather than an investigation into emergent biological phenomena. The integration of diverse data modalities across seven cell lines introduces severe feasibility risks regarding batch effects and platform artifacts.
original_review_text: This proposal aims to construct multimodal single-cell frameworks integrating DNA, RNA, protein, and chromatin accessibility data for a set of well-characterized cancer cell lines, leveraging existing large-scale resources such as DepMap and CCLE alongside newer single-cell and imaging datasets. The rationale of using homogeneous model systems to reduce donor and cell-type confounders is sound and addresses a genuine gap in current multi-omics benchmarking efforts, which typically rely on heterogeneous patient-derived samples. The project is squarely a data synthesis effort, drawing exclusively on public datasets and requiring integration across modalities that have not previously been unified computationally for these specific cell lines. However, as reviewers whose expertise centers on intrinsically disordered proteins, condensate biology, and polymer-physics-based descriptions of molecular ensembles, we find the proposal's connection to emergent phenomena in molecular and cellular biosciences to be somewhat indirect. The work is framed primarily as infrastructure and benchmarking resource development (pipeline construction, data alignment, cross-modality frameworks) rather than as an investigation of a specific emergent biological principle. While regulatory network emergence and cellular resource allocation are gestured toward as downstream applications, the central deliverable reads more as a technical/engineering resource than a hypothesis-driven inquiry into how molecular-scale interactions give rise to higher-order cellular behavior. The scope, spanning 7 cell lines and multiple layered omics types (single-cell RNA, protein imaging, chromatin accessibility, perturbation screens), appears ambitious relative to a typical working group timeline, and the proposal does not clearly detail how the team will handle known challenges such as batch effects, platform-specific artifacts, and non-identical cell subsets across independently generated datasets (imaging vs. sequencing vs. accessibility assays are rarely paired at single-cell resolution for the same cells). The team composition (machine learning, network biology, genomics) is appropriate for the computational integration task, and the project would clearly benefit from NCEMS-level data wrangling support given the scale and heterogeneity of source datasets. Open science commitments are mentioned only generically; a more explicit data/code release plan, adherence to community ontologies for omics data, and reproducibility standards would strengthen the proposal. Overall the proposal is a reasonable and useful infrastructure-building effort but is less compelling as a synthesis project targeted at answering a specific, novel scientific question about emergence, and the ambition of unifying so many data modalities across seven cell lines raises feasibility concerns within a constrained project period.

justification_relevance_to_emergent_phen: The project is relevant to emergence insofar as it aims to connect genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, chromatin, imaging, and perturbation data to understand regulatory mechanisms and cellular resource allocation. These are system-level properties that can emerge from interactions among molecular layers. However, the proposal does not articulate a precise emergent phenomenon or mechanistic hypothesis, so the connection remains implicit rather than central.
justification_novelty_and_significance: The significance is high because public cell-line resources such as DepMap and CCLE are widely used, and better multimodal integration would benefit many investigators. The novelty lies in focusing multimodal integration on deeply characterized, relatively homogeneous cell-line systems rather than heterogeneous tissue or donor benchmarks. The idea is not entirely new, as multimodal integration and benchmarking are active fields, but the cell-line-centered synthesis could be a distinctive and useful contribution.
justification_rigor_of_approach: The broad approach is plausible, but the proposal lacks critical methodological details. It does not specify integration algorithms, benchmarking criteria, treatment of batch effects, metadata normalization, uncertainty propagation, or validation strategies. For a project that depends heavily on data reuse and cross-assay comparability, these details are essential. The rigor could be strong if implemented carefully, but the current proposal does not provide enough evidence.
justification_scope_and_timeline: Restricting the project to seven cell lines is a sensible way to bound the scope, but the planned integration across bulk omics, single-cell omics, imaging, loss-of-function screens, and Perturb-seq is still ambitious. Without named datasets and staged milestones, it is difficult to judge whether the project can be completed within a working-group timeframe. A phased plan beginning with a smaller number of modalities or cell lines would improve feasibility.
justification_synthesis_focus: The proposal is strongly synthesis-focused because it relies on public data integration and does not propose new experimental data generation. It clearly requires combining distinct datasets across modalities and platforms. The project also appears to benefit from collaborative expertise beyond a single lab. The score is not higher because the synthesis plan is described at a high level and lacks details on provenance, harmonization, and reusable workflows.
justification_data_identification: The proposal names major resources such as DepMap, CCLE, perturbation datasets, and Perturb-seq, but it does not identify specific accessions, cell lines, assays, imaging datasets, or inclusion criteria. The availability and compatibility of the required single-cell and imaging data for each of the seven cell lines are not demonstrated. More explicit dataset inventories and metadata plans are needed.
justification_open_science_commitment: The proposal states that tools and resources will be delivered for the community, which suggests an open-science orientation. However, it does not specify repositories, licenses, workflow systems, containerization, documentation practices, versioning, metadata standards, governance, or long-term maintenance. Training and community engagement are also not described in detail. The commitment is directionally appropriate but under-specified.

review_text: The proposal outlines a synthesis project aimed at integrating fragmented public multiomics data across model cell lines to create a community benchmarking resource. The approach leverages existing public datasets and team expertise to reduce biological confounding and enable precise analyses of regulatory relationships. The methodology presents risks regarding assay heterogeneity and computational alignment strategies across broad unprioritized modalities.
strengths_text: The project addresses data fragmentation by integrating diverse omics imaging and perturbation datasets into a valuable benchmarking resource. The focus on well studied cell lines minimizes biological confounding and supports robust applications of the team expertise in machine learning and network biology.
weakness_text: The broad scope encompasses numerous unprioritized datasets and modalities creating significant risks for computational alignment and batch effect management. The methodology relies heavily on imputation assumptions for cross modality integration and prioritizes resource generation over targeted biological discovery or reproducible community governance frameworks.
original_review_text:
This proposal addresses an important and timely problem: the fragmentation of public multi-omics data for widely used cancer and model cell lines. The central idea, to build integrated multimodal frameworks for a small set of cell lines with deep public profiling across DNA, chromatin, RNA, protein, imaging, and perturbation datasets, is well aligned with synthesis research and could generate a valuable community benchmarking resource. The focus on matched or near-matched model systems is a useful contrast to many current multimodal benchmarks, which are dominated by heterogeneous tissue or donor-derived samples. If executed well, the work could enable more precise analyses of regulatory relationships, genotype-to-phenotype links, and cellular responses to perturbation.

However, the proposal as presented remains high-level and under-specified. It does not identify the seven cell lines, the exact public datasets to be integrated, the metadata standards to be used, or the criteria for inclusion and quality control. The phrase "within the same cell" is potentially misleading unless the datasets truly contain joint measurements in the same single cells; otherwise, the project will depend heavily on computational alignment, imputation, or latent-variable modeling across unmatched assays. The computational strategy is also not described in sufficient detail: it is unclear how batch effects, platform-specific biases, copy number effects, protein/RNA discordance, missing modalities, perturbation context, and benchmarking ground truth will be handled. The proposal would benefit from a more explicit distinction between resource construction, biological discovery, and methods benchmarking, with concrete deliverables and evaluation metrics for each. Open science commitments are mentioned only generally, and trainee training and community engagement are not described in detail.

Overall, this is a promising synthesis-oriented project with potentially broad utility, but the current description lacks the methodological and data-management specificity needed to fully assess feasibility and rigor.

The approach leverages existing public datasets and team expertise to reduce biological confounding and enable precise analyses of regulatory relationships. The methodology presents risks regarding assay heterogeneity and computational alignment strategies across broad unprioritized modalities.
rephrased_strengths: The project addresses data fragmentation by integrating diverse omics imaging and perturbation datasets into a valuable benchmarking resource. The focus on well studied cell lines minimizes biological confounding and supports robust applications of the team expertise in machine learning and network biology.
rephrased_weakness: The broad scope encompasses numerous unprioritized datasets and modalities creating significant risks for computational alignment and batch effect management. The methodology relies heavily on imputation assumptions for cross modality integration and prioritizes resource generation over targeted biological discovery or reproducible community governance frameworks.

justification_data_identification: The proposal names major data sources and data classes, including DepMap, CCLE, loss-of-function screens, Perturb-seq, single-cell multi-omics, and imaging data. original_review_text:
This proposal addresses an important and timely problem: the fragmented state of publicly available bulk, single-cell, perturbational, and imaging-derived multi-omics data for widely used cancer and model cell lines. The central idea of building cell-line-specific multimodal frameworks that align DNA, chromatin accessibility, RNA, protein, imaging, and perturbation data is well matched to a synthesis-focused funding mechanism. The proposal is strongest as a community resource and benchmark-building effort, with potential to enable mechanistic studies of gene regulation, proteome allocation, and perturbation responses in controlled cellular contexts. The focus on commonly used cell lines is a compelling design choice because it reduces donor and cell-type heterogeneity and may allow more precise cross-modality inference than current heterogeneous multimodal benchmarks. From the perspective of systems-level molecular and cellular biology, the proposal could contribute to understanding emergent regulatory behavior, especially how genomic, epigenomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic layers combine to produce stable cellular states and responses to perturbation.

However, the proposal as written remains high level. It does not sufficiently define the scientific questions that will be answered beyond creating a resource and computational pipelines. Terms such as "model and quantify DNA, RNA, and protein within the same cell," "regulatory mechanisms," and "cellular resource allocation" are potentially important but underdeveloped. It is not clear whether the team will infer causal regulatory networks, benchmark imputation across modalities, model cell-state heterogeneity, predict perturbation responses, or discover general principles of cross-layer regulation. The proposal would be strengthened by specifying testable hypotheses, quantitative success criteria, and concrete analytical methods. For example, it should describe how single-cell and bulk data will be aligned despite differences in platform, batch, measurement sparsity, temporal state, and protein coverage; how uncertainty will be propagated; and how inferred regulatory relationships will be validated using independent public perturbation data. The selection criteria for the seven cell lines are also not described, and it is unclear whether the needed public datasets exist at sufficient depth and comparability for each selected line.

The project fits the public-data synthesis requirement well, and the need for coordinated data wrangling, benchmarking, and community standards is plausible. Still, the proposal would benefit from a more explicit explanation of why NCEMS support is essential beyond conventional computational biology collaboration. Open science is mentioned through delivery of tools and a benchmarking resource, but the proposal should provide a stronger plan for versioned data products, reproducible workflows, metadata standards, containerized pipelines, community governance, and training of trainees. Overall, this is a significant and fundable synthesis concept with strong relevance to multimodal cellular systems biology, but it needs sharper scientific framing and more methodological detail to rise from a valuable data-integration resource to a compelling study of emergent molecular and cellular phenomena.
rephrased_review: The proposal presents a fundable data integration concept with overly broad scientific framing and methodological details. The creation of a community benchmark integrating diverse data modalities for homogeneous cell lines facilitates the study of regulatory behavior. The hypotheses and analytical methods remain generalized while the cell line selection relies on assumed data availability.
rephrased_strengths: Integrating genomic and proteomic measurements with imaging and perturbation data creates a valuable community resource for studying model systems. Focusing on heavily studied cell lines reduces donor and cell type heterogeneity to enable precise regulatory relationship inference.
rephrased_weakness: The biological questions and analytical frameworks regarding data harmonization and causal inference rely on generalized descriptions. The target cell line selection assumes comprehensive data availability while the open science and training components consist of preliminary concepts.

original_review_text:
This proposal addresses an important and timely problem: the fragmentation of extensive public multi-omics data for widely used cancer and model cell lines. The idea of focusing on a limited set of cell lines with unusually rich bulk, single-cell, perturbational, and imaging datasets is attractive because it could reduce some confounding sources of donor and cell-type heterogeneity and enable sharper questions about cross-layer relationships among genotype, chromatin accessibility, RNA abundance, protein abundance, and perturbation response. The proposal is well aligned with the synthesis mission in that it relies on existing public datasets and would likely require substantial collaborative data harmonization across genomics, machine learning, and network biology. If successful, the resulting benchmark resource and workflows could be valuable to a broad community.

However, the proposal as presented reads more as a resource-integration and benchmarking effort than as a sharply articulated synthesis project centered on a fundamental biological question or emergent phenomenon. The abstract mentions regulatory mechanisms and cellular resource allocation, but it does not define specific testable questions, expected models, validation criteria, or examples of long-standing puzzles that the integrated framework will resolve. The central methodological challenge is also underdeveloped: most of the proposed data types will not be measured in the same physical cells, so the claim of quantifying DNA, RNA, and protein within the same cell requires careful qualification and a rigorous statistical strategy for cross-modal alignment. The proposal would be stronger if it specified the seven cell lines, enumerated the exact public datasets to be integrated, described quality-control and batch-effect strategies, and defined quantitative benchmarks for success. Overall, this is a potentially useful synthesis effort with strong relevance to public multi-omics integration, but it needs a clearer scientific hypothesis and a more detailed analytic plan to fully meet the ambitions of the call.

The project aligns with synthesis objectives by proposing community benchmarks and leveraging existing data resources across genomics and network biology. The broad integration approach carries analytical risks regarding the statistical alignment of diverse data modalities across separate experiments and the management of biological variation.
rephrased_strengths: Focusing on a limited number of cell lines provides a strategy to reduce confounding heterogeneity and enable precise data comparisons. The planned resource offers valuable benchmarks for multimodal modeling and regulatory network inference while leveraging appropriate computational expertise.
rephrased_weakness: The project emphasizes broad resource integration over fundamental biological hypotheses. The analytical framework entails complex statistical matching across separate experiments and carries significant risks regarding the management of biological variation and batch effects.

original_review_text:
This proposal addresses an important and timely problem: the integration of publicly available bulk, single-cell, imaging, perturbation, and multi-omic datasets for widely used cell line systems. The focus on cell lines is a notable strength because these systems have unusually deep public characterization through resources such as DepMap and CCLE, and reduced donor and cell-type heterogeneity could enable more interpretable cross-modal alignment than heterogeneous tissue atlases. A well-executed project could produce a valuable benchmarking and analysis resource for understanding relationships among genome state, chromatin accessibility, RNA abundance, protein abundance, perturbation response, and cellular resource allocation. The proposal is well aligned with synthesis research in that it relies on existing public datasets and would require expertise spanning machine learning, genomics, network biology, and data engineering.

However, the proposal remains quite high-level and does not provide enough detail to evaluate feasibility or scientific rigor with confidence. The seven cell lines are not named, the specific datasets are not enumerated, and it is unclear whether the proposed modalities are available in sufficiently comparable conditions, batches, platforms, and perturbational contexts for each selected line. The phrase “model and quantify DNA, RNA, and protein within the same cell” is ambitious, but most public data sources will not directly measure all of these modalities in the same physical cells; the proposal should distinguish clearly between true multimodal single-cell measurements, computational co-embedding, label transfer, and bulk-informed imputation. The computational strategy is also underdeveloped: no specific modeling framework, validation scheme, benchmark metrics, uncertainty quantification, or plan for batch correction and platform harmonization is described. The proposal would be stronger if it articulated a small number of testable biological questions, such as whether chromatin accessibility and copy number jointly predict transcriptional and protein-level buffering, or whether perturbation effects propagate reproducibly across molecular layers. As written, it risks becoming primarily a data-wrangling and benchmarking exercise rather than a synthesis project that directly answers compelling questions about emergent molecular and cellular behavior.

The project appears appropriate for NCEMS support because the integration of many public datasets across modalities and cell lines is beyond the scope of a typical single laboratory. Still, the proposal provides limited information on the working group structure, trainee involvement, timeline, deliverables, community engagement, and open-science governance. Overall, this is a promising concept with clear relevance to public-data synthesis and computational molecular systems biology, but it requires greater specificity about data sources, methods, validation, biological questions, and community outputs to be fully compelling.

The use of homogeneous model systems with deep existing characterization provides a foundation for assessing cross modal regulatory relationships. The broad formulation of the biological questions limits the evaluation of data comparability, analytical frameworks and project governance.
rephrased_strengths: Targeting homogeneous cell line models minimizes confounding donor variation and facilitates the analysis of regulatory interactions. Integrating public datasets with established resources like DepMap establishes a community benchmark for connecting molecular states to functional phenotypes.
rephrased_weakness: The generalized description of the datasets restricts the evaluation of measurement comparability across different biological conditions and technical platforms. The emphasis on broad resource creation limits the assessment of specific computational algorithms, validation metrics and project timelines.
